34.0.0.en: 1 The hopes of a man void of understanding are vain and false: and dreams lift up fools. 2 Whoso regardeth dreams is like him that catcheth at a shadow, and followeth after the wind. 3 The vision of dreams is the resemblance of one thing to another, as the likeness of a man before a man's face. 4 Of an unclean thing what can be cleansed? and from that thing that is false what truth can come? 5 Divinations, and soothsayings, and dreams, are vain. 6 And the heart fancieth, as a woman's heart in travail. If they be not sent from the most High in thy visitation, set not thy heart upon them. 7 For dreams have deceived many, and they have failed that put their trust in them. 8 The law shall be found perfect without lies: and wisdom is perfection to a faithful mouth. 9 A man that is instructed knoweth many things; and he that hath much experience will speak with understanding.

34.0.1.en: The ancient Greeks often thought of dreams as messages from the gods. As for the Jews, dreams appear in the Old Testament carrying messages from God, and warnings are also given against vain, deceptive dreams.

34.0.2.en: The Old Testament mentions the dreams that Joseph the son of Jacob saw: in his youth he saw two dreams; in prison he interpreted two dreams for the king's cupbearer and the king's baker; and in the palace he interpreted two dreams for Pharaoh king of Egypt. These six dreams were from God and were actually fulfilled. In the New Testament Joseph the carpenter saw three dreams: the first after the Incarnation of the Word in the Virgin (Mt 1:25), the second for the flight to Egypt with the Child Jesus and His mother, and the third concerning the return from Egypt. As for Daniel, who was nearer to Ben Sirach in time, he was known as a man of dreams; he interpreted many dreams that declared God's plan and included prophecies that were fulfilled in history, and others that prophesied of the coming of the Lord Christ and His second coming.

34.0.3.en: Nevertheless, the foolish person gives himself over to vain dreams and puts his hope in them.

34.0.4.en: The prophets of old warned much against the error into which dreams can lead, and stressed not relying on them, especially since a confusion had occurred between them and divination, sorcery and charlatanry. "I have heard what the prophets said, that prophesy lies in my name, saying, I have dreamed, I have dreamed. How long shall this be in the heart of the prophets that prophesy lies? yea, they are prophets of the deceit of their own heart; which think to cause my people to forget my name by their dreams which they tell every man to his neighbour, as their fathers have forgotten my name for Baal. The prophet that hath a dream, let him tell a dream; and he that hath my word, let him speak my word faithfully. What is the chaff to the wheat? saith the LORD" (Jer 23:25-28; cf. Deut 13:2-6; Eccl 5:6-7; Jer 29:8-9; 27:9-11; Zech 10:2) [1].

34.0.5.en: The man without understanding has futile and false hopes, and dreams give wings to those without understanding [1].

34.0.6.en: Corrupt souls, turned aside from the truth, place their hope not in returning to God with a pure heart, an upright life and sincere repentance, but in a vain hope that relies on deceptive dreams.

34.1.0.en: One who pays attention to dreams is like one who grasps at shadows and pursues the wind [2].

34.2.0.en: He who walks after the vain world has vain dreams; he clings to them like one who grasps at shadows, and runs after them as after the wind [5].

34.2.1.en: The vision of dreams is this over against that, and the likeness of face before face [3].

34.2.2.en: A dream is often merely a reflection of events or imaginings, like the reflection of a man's face in a mirror, as though it did not represent a real existence.

34.2.3.en: What can be cleansed from an unclean thing?

34.2.4.en: And what truth can come from a false thing? [4]

34.2.5.en: We shall not profit from dreams unless our depths are purified, so that God works in us.

34.2.6.en: He does not mean that all dreams are unclean, but he gives an example: if what is unclean produces nothing pure, so also what appears in a dream does not represent a reality, but is vain and false; can falsehood then produce truth?!

34.2.7.en: Divination, omens (augury) and dreams are worthless, like a woman in the pains of labor, the heart becomes visible [5].

34.2.8.en: Ben Sirach sees that seeking after divination, omens and dreams reveals a person's inner disturbance and instability, and the Law forbade them explicitly (Lev 19:26; Deut 18:10-14). While they were counted unfitting for the believer (1 Sam 6:2; Isa 44:25; Ezek 13:6-8; 21:26), the pagans practiced them. Ben Sirach made clear that man's mind pictures divination, omens and vain dreams out of itself, and he thereby highlights the psychological aspect that modern psychologists proclaim.

34.3.0.en: If visions are not sent from the Most High in a visitation from Him, do not set your heart upon them [6].

34.3.1.en: The pious, wise person discerns the dreams and visions that come from the Most High, and opens his heart to them, so that divination, omens and false dreams do not lead him astray.

34.4.0.en: For dreams have led many astray, and those who put their hope in them have fallen [7].

34.4.1.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the images that appear in dreams affect the soul and arise in different ways, so they must be discerned [2]: 1. Sometimes dreams occur because of indigestion. 2. Sometimes they occur as the fruit of illusory imaginings that occupy a person's mind. 3. Sometimes a dream is a revelation of something. 4. There are dreams stirred up by the enemy of good, the devil; therefore Holy Scripture warns us: "For dreams have deceived many, and they have failed that put their trust in them" [7]. It also commanded us: "Neither shall ye use enchantment, nor observe times" (Lev 19:26). 5. There are dreams that are holy revelations. Pope Gregory (the Great) says: [In any case, the saints, by the discernment they have acquired, are able to distinguish between illusions and revelations, and to penetrate the meaning of the words and images in visions. Thus they know what is from the good Spirit and what is from deceptive imaginings. But if the soul is not prudent in the matter of dreams, it finds itself perished in a forest of vanity that is the work of the deceiving spirit, who by his art sometimes presents many true things, and afterward captures it in the snare of a single lie.]

34.4.2.en: Some scholars also see that dreams are often a reflection of what is within a person, of scenes, events and imaginings, when a person sleeps and the censor over the unconscious is weak. Some are the fruit of sleeping in an uncomfortable position. Some are the fruit of a person's intense preoccupation with a matter all day long, especially in the period immediately before sleep. Sometimes dreams reflect some events or behaviors of the person when he was a child or a youth, which he no longer remembers. And some dreams are deceptions of the enemy of good against a person in order to lead him astray.

34.5.0.en: The Law is fulfilled without such lies, and wisdom is perfect in the mouth of the believer [8].

34.5.1.en: Ben Sirach affirms that the Law, as the source of true wisdom, is a safeguard for the believer, who draws from it instead of resorting to deceptive superstitions.

34.6.s.en: 2. Practical experiences and the benefit of travels

34.6.0.en: 10 He that hath no experience knoweth little: but he that hath travelled is full of prudence. 11 He that hath not been tried, what doth he know? and he that hath wandered is full of cunning. 12 I have seen many things in my wanderings, and most of my words come from what I have experienced. 13 Often have I ventured myself in this pursuit, even unto death, and then I escaped.

34.6.1.en: The man who travels much knows much, and the one of much experience speaks with understanding [9].

34.6.2.en: If the Law keeps the believer from the deception of illusions and dreams, it nevertheless does not prevent the believer from benefiting from the experience of others. For the Law purifies the heart and the mind, and urges the believer to resort to God with reverence and piety. In this way the believer benefits from his many travels, for he enjoys a spirit of discernment, and so perceives what is true and distinguishes it from what is false.

34.6.3.en: He who has not been tried knows little, but he who travels increases in prudence [10].

34.7.0.en: I have seen many things in my travels, and what I understood is more than I can express in words [11].

34.7.1.en: God is able to make known His will and counsel by many means, among them travels, to those who are sanctified to Him.

34.8.0.en: Often I was exposed to the danger of death, and I escaped because of those experiences [12].

34.8.1.en: Although Ben Sirach valued learning from the experience of others, which requires travel to meet with different cultures and experiences, he was confident in the Lord who rescued him as from death [12]. He presented his experience of benefiting from the experience of others, and his practical experience of trusting in God who saves and cares for him, so that he is not terrified of anything and fears no one.

34.8.2.en: v [And bring us not into temptation] In some manuscripts "and lead us not" occurs, and it is equivalent to "bring us not in," because the Greek word carries both meanings. Some pray, saying: "Do not allow us to be led into temptation." For God does not lead a person into temptation, but He permits the one who has been deprived of His help to be led into it, according to God's hidden wisdom and according to the merits of the one whom He allows to be led into temptation.

34.8.3.en: To be led into temptation differs from a person's being tested. For without temptation no man is approved. He is tried to approve himself, as it is written: "He that hath not been tried, what doth he know?" (cf. Sir 34:11), or he is tried to approve others, as the Apostle says: "Your temptation[3] which was in my flesh ye despised not" (Gal 4:14). For from these circumstances the Apostle knew that they were steadfast, because they did not abandon love on account of the troubles that befell the Apostle in the flesh. As for God, He knows us before we are tried, for He knows all things before they come to be [4].

34.9.s.en: 3. The fear of the Lord, a harbor of safety

34.9.0.en: 14 The spirit of those that fear the Lord shall live, 15 for their hope is in him that saveth them. 16 Whoso feareth the Lord shall not fear nor be afraid, for he is his hope. 17 Whoso feareth the Lord, blessed is his soul. 18 To whom doth he look? and who is his stay? 19 For the eyes of the Lord are upon them that love him, he is a mighty protector and a strong stay, a covering from the heat and a shadow from the noonday sun. 20 A defence from stumbling and a help when falling. He lifteth up the soul and lighteneth the eyes: he giveth health, life and blessing.

34.9.1.en: What occupies Ben Sirach in the matter of vain dreams is to reveal the safe way for ordering the believer's life:

34.9.2.en: a. He highlighted the necessity of enjoying a spirit of discernment in order to be rid of pagan practices such as divination, omens and the interpretation of deceptive dreams [5].

34.9.3.en: b. Holding fast to the Law to enjoy perfect wisdom [8].

34.9.4.en: c. Benefiting from the experiences of others through travels.

34.9.5.en: d. Sure hope is realized through the fear of the Lord, as a harbor of safety from every deception, whatever its source, whether the illusions of the soul, or slipping into pagan practices, or the deception of the enemy of good through misleading dreams.

34.9.6.en: Now he speaks of the fear of the Lord and its work in the believer's life: 1. The fear of the Lord gives life to the spirit that sin kills [13]. 2. The fear of the Lord gives a spirit of challenge, so that one fears nothing and is not terrified [14-15]. 3. The fear of the Lord shows us that the eyes of the Lord are toward those who love Him and keep them from every danger [16]. 4. The fear of the Lord lifts the soul and gives it inner insight, healing, life and blessing [17].

34.9.7.en: St. Mar Philoxenus recorded for us two homilies (memre) on the fear of the Lord, after writing two on faith and two on simplicity. He presented to us the fear of the Lord as a person born of faith and keeper of faith. He made clear that Adam, and after him Cain, drove the fear of the Lord away from themselves, and so lost their faith.

34.9.8.en: Those who fear the Lord, their spirit lives, for their hope is in Him who saves them [13].

34.9.9.en: v He who understands what the body is, that is, that it is corruptible and short-lived, understands also that the soul is heavenly and immortal, that it is a breath from God, and is joined to the body until it advances and rises toward likeness to God. The man who understands the soul rightly walks in an upright life that pleases God, and is wary of the body and does not trifle with it. Likewise, by the mind's contemplation of God, he sees mentally (spiritually) the eternal blessings that God gives to the soul [5].

34.9.10.en: St. Anthony the Great He who fears the Lord fears nothing and is never terrified, because the Lord is his hope [14].

34.9.11.en: v Because Cain did not fear God willingly, fear ruled over him by compulsion, and he became terrified, a wanderer on the face of the earth, and under the torment of fear he was begging God to make any man kill him, that he might be rid of this life full of fear and terror!

34.9.12.en: St. Mar Philoxenus of Mabbug Blessed is the soul of the man who fears the Lord.

34.10.0.en: To whom does he look? And who is his support? [15]

34.10.1.en: v The test of the fear of the Lord is within the soul; and only the man himself can know whether he fears God or not. Have you remembered God and trembled? Have you thought of Him and been filled with fear? Have your thoughts trembled along with your members, and your soul with your body? Has your mind bowed your head, and has shame come upon you before God? If these things happen to you, know that the fear of the Lord is in you, and the remembrance of God is indeed present with you [6].

34.10.2.en: St. Mar Philoxenus of Mabbug The eyes of the Lord are on those who love Him. He is an effective protection and a strong support:

34.11.0.en: He is a refuge from the heat of the scorching, and a shade from the noonday sun, a protection from stumbling, and a help from falling [16].

34.11.1.en: Ben Sirach calls those who fear the Lord "those who love Him." He who loves the Lord finds his protection in the Lord, for He supports him from the heat of temptations, saves him from falling, glorifies him, enlightens his inner insight, gives him healing from sorrows, and gladdens his heart with His divine goods. If the Lord is called the Sun of righteousness who enlightens the soul, then the enemy of good is called Satan, in that he pushes men toward burning temptations. Fear supports the believer in his striving against evil, especially in his resisting inner thoughts:

34.11.2.en: v The fear of the Lord is the bridle that stops a person's rush toward committing evil, and pulls him back when he is enslaved to running after his loathsome desires, not only in his outward life but especially in his hidden inner life" [6: 181].

34.11.3.en: v The man who lives in the remembrance of God at all times is filled with fear, even when resisting a thought of lust that passes over his soul, and he becomes terrified because of this thought. But the thought flees at once before the fear of the soul, like a bird that flees from the man who disturbs its rest. Fear and respect for men's laws keep the body from lusts. And fear and a man's shame before God keep the soul from evil thoughts. For when he knows that God sees him at all times, he watches himself continually lest he sin [7].

34.11.4.en: St. Mar Philoxenus of Mabbug (The Lord) raises the soul up [8], enlightens the eyes, and gives healing, life and blessing [17].

34.11.5.en: v As fear accompanies the childhood of this world and drives it to learn reading and writing, so also the fear of the Lord suits the childhood of the soul, and drives it to carry out the commandments and not to treat the word of God lightly [9].

34.12.0.en: 21 He that sacrificeth of a thing wrongfully gotten, his offering is mocked; and the mockeries of the wicked are not well pleasing. 22 The Lord is alone for those that wait for him in the way of truth and righteousness. 23 The most High is not pleased with the offerings of the hypocrites; neither is he pacified for their sins by the multitude of their sacrifices. 24 Whoso bringeth an offering of the goods of the poor doeth as one that killeth the son before his father. 25 The bread of the needy is their life: he that withholdeth it from them is a shedder of blood. 26 He that snatcheth his neighbour's living slayeth him. 27 He that withholdeth the hire of the hireling sheddeth his blood. 28 One buildeth and another pulleth down; what profit have they but labour? 29 One prayeth and another curseth; whose prayer will the Lord hear? 30 He that is washed from the touching of the dead and toucheth it again, what availeth his washing? 31 So is a man that fasteth for his sins and doeth them again: who will hear his prayer, and what hath his humbling profited him?

34.12.1.en: Of all the wisdom books, Ben Sirach alone is concerned to speak of the true worship of God. From the beginning of the book the writer declared his concern for the service of the Lord (2:1). In his view the service of the Lord is the true life of man.

34.12.2.en: The service of the Lord is bound up with the believer's inner life. Like the prophet Isaiah, Ben Sirach perceives that worship and the offering of sacrifices can be practiced with a letter that has no spirit, and so the Lord is not pleased with them; stopping at the letter without purity of heart is a disdain of living communion with the Lord. Like Isaiah, Sirach links the offering of sacrifices with walking in the fear of the Lord [18, 20]. Sirach gives examples of worship and offerings unacceptable to the Lord.

34.12.3.en: He who approaches the Lord with his heart isolated from his brethren, the Lord will not accept him. The first murder in the world took place during Cain's offerings to the Lord, which were not accepted (cf. Gen 4:3-5). It is to be noted that Luke the Evangelist, who spoke much of prayer, also spoke much of almsgiving. For by practical love and works of mercy and compassion, God smells prayer as a sweet savour of acceptance. Therefore the Lord warned us against offering sacrifices on the altar before we are reconciled with our brethren.

34.12.4.en: He who offers sacrifices by committing iniquity, the offering is mockery; and the gifts of the wicked are not accepted [18].

34.12.5.en: The Most High is not pleased with the offerings of the wicked, nor by the multitude of their sacrifices does a man obtain forgiveness of his sins [19].

34.12.6.en: He who offers a sacrifice from the possessions of the poor slays a son before his father [20].

34.12.7.en: v He who has turned to bitterness because of the roots of deadly poison cannot bring forth sweet fruit. For this reason the Lord says by the prophet, rejecting even the offerings: "For I the LORD love judgment, I hate robbery for burnt offering" (Isa 61:8). He also says: "The sacrifice of the wicked is abomination: how much more, when he bringeth it with a wicked mind?" (Prov 21:27). They offer to God even the things they take from the needy, but the Lord shows with great reproof how He strips them, saying by the wise man: "Whoso bringeth an offering of the goods of the poor doeth as one that killeth the son before his father" (cf. Sir 34:20). And is there anything more dreadful than killing the son before the eyes of his father? So God looks upon these sacrifices with great wrath, like the grief of a father who has lost his son [10].

34.12.9.en: The bread of the needy is the life of the poor, and he who deprives them of it is a shedder of blood [21].

34.13.0.en: He who takes away his neighbor's living slays him, and he who deprives the hireling of his wages sheds his blood [22].

34.14.0.en: If one builds and another pulls down, what do they gain but labor? [23]

34.14.1.en: The statements [23-26] highlight the continual struggle between good and evil. It is good for a man to fast and pray in order to obtain forgiveness, but he must not become careless and fall into that for which he offered repentance.

34.14.2.en: St. Barsanuphius was asked: If a person is not sincere in his repentance, will his sins be forgiven for the sake of the saints if they pray for him? The saint used this saying, counting the saints as building by their prayers, while the one who is careless in his repentance pulls down, so what is the gain but labor?

34.14.3.en: v The man who does not practice what he is able to do, and relied on this effort, that is, the prayers of the saints, their prayers do not profit him at all. If they practiced the ascetic life and prayed for him while he lived a life of waste and dissoluteness, what is the benefit of their prayers to him? For the saying is fulfilled: "When one buildeth, and another pulleth down, what profit have they then but labour?!" (cf. Sir 34:23).

34.14.4.en: Truly, if it were possible for this to happen, that is, for the saints to pray for a man and he be saved, while the latter did not care about it even with a little concern, then nothing would have prevented them from doing so for the sins of the world [11].

34.14.5.en: St. Barsanuphius v In truth, if those who build are many and the one who pulls down is one, destruction is easy and breaks the many hands of the builders [12].

34.15.0.en: St. John Chrysostom When one prayeth, and another curseth, whose voice will the Lord hear? [24]

34.15.1.en: v A man who takes from what belongs to others and gives it to another does not show mercy, but practices great error and injustice.

34.15.2.en: And as a stone cannot bring forth oil, so cruelty does not bring mercy. When almsgiving is practiced in this way it is not counted as almsgiving. Therefore I urge you not only to consider how we give to the needy, but also not to give from what we have taken from others.

34.15.3.en: When one prayeth, and another curseth, whose voice will the Lord hear?" (cf. Sir 34:24).

34.15.4.en: If we guide ourselves so strictly, we shall be able, by the grace of God, to obtain many compassions and mercies and forgiveness for all that we did throughout the long time, and to flee to the Kingdom of Heaven by the grace and compassion of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen [13].

34.16.0.en: St. John Chrysostom He that washeth himself after the touching of a dead body, and toucheth it again, what availeth his washing? [25]

34.16.1.en: v If a man gives his wealth to God, but offers himself to Satan, he fulfills what is written: "He that washeth himself after the touching of a dead body, and toucheth it again, what availeth his washing?" (cf. Sir 34:25). Likewise the Apostle Peter made clear: "For if after they have escaped the pollutions of the world ... they are again entangled therein, and overcome, the latter end is worse with them than the beginning" (2 Pet 2:20).

34.16.2.en: Consider, brethren, the testimony of the blessed Peter concerning sinners: if, after they have begun to be saved from their sins, they return to the mire of vice, their last state becomes worse than the first. What the same Apostle Peter added points to the same people: "The dog is turned to his own vomit again; and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire" (2 Pet 2:22). In fact Solomon (Ben Sirach) warns us more clearly in more terrifying words: "My son, hast thou sinned? do so no more, but pray for thy former sins, and they shall be forgiven thee" (cf. Sir 21:1) [14].

34.16.3.en: v Beloved, dear ones, do not allow the divine blessings to be destroyed in you by your following evil deeds, lest vices overtake you unawares, and virtues do not leave your hearts. For what is written is fulfilled: "He that washeth himself after the touching of a dead body, and toucheth it again, what availeth his washing?" (cf. Sir 34:25).

34.16.4.en: If the virtues withdraw and we accept the vices, we must fear the fulfillment of the words: "When the unclean spirit is gone out of a man, he walketh through dry places, seeking rest, and findeth none. Then he saith, I will return into my house from whence I came out; and when he is come, he findeth it empty, swept, and garnished. Then goeth he, and taketh with himself seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and they enter in and dwell there: and the last state of that man is worse than the first" (Mt 12:43-45) [15].

34.16.5.en: v According to the greatness of what we receive, it befits us to guard it with more care and attention. It is a grave matter for a pagan to reject the grace of God, but the danger is no less if a Christian, after having received it, returns and loses it. It is not the dignity of the title "Christian" that makes him a Christian. You have no profit at all in the title itself unless you show it by works. So the Lord Himself also says in the Gospel: "And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?" (Lk 6:46). Therefore let us strive to live in purity, righteousness and godliness, so that when we stand before the judgment seat of the eternal Judge, we are not punished with the wicked and sinners, but are made worthy to receive the eternal rewards with the righteous who fear God, by the help of our Lord, to whom belong honor and power forever and ever. Amen [16].

34.16.6.en: Fr. Caesarius, Bishop of Arles v Those who do not keep the innocence of life after lamentation neglect purity after washing. And those who wash but are not cleansed are none other than those who commit the sins over which they were weeping and still are. Therefore the wise man says: "He that washeth himself after the touching of a dead body, and toucheth it again, what availeth his washing?" (cf. Sir 34:25).

34.16.7.en: He who purifies himself by weeping is like the one who washes after touching the dead, while he who returns to commit sin after shedding tears over it is like one who returns to touching the dead after his washing. Those who mourn over their sins but do not leave them ought to know that in the eye of the just Judge they are like those who, when they stand before certain persons, grieve with humble supplication, but when they leave them, bear them all hatred and harm [17].

34.16.9.en: v Such people do not wash away their sins by their sighs, since they do not cease sinning after their sighing. They sigh because of their crimes, and after sighing they return to them. Of these the Holy Scripture says in the Book of Ben Sirach: "He that washeth himself after the touching of a dead body, and toucheth it again, what availeth his washing? So is it with a man that fasteth for his sins, and doeth the same again: who will hear his prayer?" (cf. Sir 34:25-26). Therefore God rightly says to men: "By returning and sighing ye shall be saved" (cf. Isa 30:15) [18].

34.16.11.en: So is it with a man that fasteth for his sins, and doeth the same again: who will hear his prayer?

34.17.0.en: And what doth his humbling profit him? [26]

34.17.1.en: v If Eve had practiced fasting and avoided eating of the fruit of this tree, we would not have been in need of this fast, because "They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick" (Mt 9:12). It is our sin that brought sickness upon us. So let us be healed by repentance; but repentance without the practice of fasting is vain: "Cursed is the ground for thy sake ... Thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee; and thou shalt eat the herb of the field" (Gen 3:17-18) [19].

34.17.2.en: St. Basil the Great Inspired by Sirach 34

34.18.s.en: Your fear is my refuge from my weaknesses

34.18.0.en: v My God, how do I distinguish between holy dreams and vain dreams?

34.18.1.en: Nail Your fear in me, that my heart may be purified by Your grace, and I may enjoy safety as You give me the spirit of discernment.

34.18.2.en: v Sanctify my mind and my heart, that in earnestness I may experience fellowship with You.

34.18.3.en: And in my travels let me learn from the experiences of my brethren with You.

34.18.4.en: v That I may fear You, O Holy One, and so fear nothing, and You open to me the door of hope, and I hide in You!

34.18.5.en: Your fear leads me to the worship that is pleasing before You.

34.18.6.en: You open to me the door of heaven, and my heart is lifted up to it.

34.18.7.en: Let my tongue offer You a sacrifice of thanksgiving, which You smell as a sweet savour of acceptance.

34.18.8.en: By Your fear I practice my fasts, my prayers and my prostrations (metanoias), and all worship, with boldness before You!
